original_value: The low communication bandwidth between memory and processing units in conventional von Neumann machines does not support the requirements of emerging applications that rely extensively on large sets of data. More recent computing paradigms, such as high parallelization and near‐memory computing, help alleviate the data communication bottleneck to some extent, but paradigm‐shifting concepts are required. In‐memory computing has emerged as a prime candidate to eliminate this bottleneck by colocating memory and processing. In this context, resistive switching (RS) memory devices is a key promising choice, due to their unique intrinsic device‐level properties, enabling both storing and computing with a small, massively‐parallel footprint at low power. Theoretically, this directly translates to a major boost in energy efficiency and computational throughput, but various practical challenges remain. A qualitative and quantitative analysis of several key existing challenges in implementing high‐capacity, high‐volume RS memories for accelerating the most computationally demanding computation in machine learning (ML) inference, that of vector‐matrix multiplication (VMM), is presented. The monolithic integration of RS memories with complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) integrated circuits is presented as the core underlying technology. The key existing design choices in terms of device‐level physical implementation, circuit‐level design, and system‐level considerations is reviewed and an outlook for future directions is provided.

result.paraphrase: Conventional von Neumann machines suffer from low communication bandwidth between memory and processing units, which cannot meet the needs of emerging applications that depend heavily on large data sets. Although newer paradigms such as high parallelization and near-memory computing ease the data-communication bottleneck to some extent, more transformative concepts are still needed. In-memory computing has emerged as a leading candidate to remove this bottleneck by colocating memory and processing. Within this framework, resistive switching (RS) memory devices are a particularly promising option because their intrinsic device-level properties support both storage and computation in a compact, massively parallel, low-power footprint. In theory, this leads directly to significant gains in energy efficiency and computational throughput, though practical challenges remain. This work presents a qualitative and quantitative analysis of several key challenges in realizing high-capacity, high-volume RS memories for accelerating the most computationally intensive operation in machine learning (ML) inference, namely vector-matrix multiplication (VMM). It also presents monolithic integration of RS memories with complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) integrated circuits as the core enabling technology, reviews the main design choices at the device, circuit, and system levels, and concludes with future directions.
